guards.rule: A room's main piece (the bed in a bedroom) must be built and visible in the render; if the build stage drops it, the stage must re-run until the piece is present.

A site area labeled in the documents (e.g. VERANDA, BALKON) must be built with an outline and structure in the model; if the site stage leaves it as an open slab, the stage must re-run until the structure is present.

A room typed as a children's room must be furnished with child-appropriate anchors (single or bunk beds, play area) rather than adult double beds; the furniture agent must respect the room's intended occupant profile when selecting bed types.

A dressing room (soyunma odası) must contain a dressing table or vanity as its primary anchor piece, not just a shoe cabinet; the furniture agent must recognize 'dressing room' as requiring a vanity/dressing table group, distinct from a simple storage or hall room.

A bathroom or shower room that includes a washing machine in its piece list must have a valid placement strategy for the appliance; if the room is too small for a standard wc_set group, the washing machine should be placed as a standalone appliance or the room type should be adjusted to allow appliance placement without requiring a full wc_set group.

Bathroom fixtures (bathtub, washbasin) must be placed at their correct working heights and visible in the render; the fit stage must verify that all listed bathroom pieces are built and positioned correctly, not just listed.
Hall rooms must have their main anchor piece (e.g., shoe cabinet) visible in the render; the fit stage must ensure that all listed hall pieces are built and positioned correctly, not just listed.
Bedroom rooms must have their main anchor piece (e.g., bed) visible in the render; the fit stage must ensure that all listed bedroom pieces are built and positioned correctly, not just listed.

Small utility or hall rooms must have their main anchor piece (e.g., shoe cabinet) visible in the render; the fit stage must ensure that all listed pieces are built and positioned correctly, not just listed.
Bathroom fixtures must use library models that are visible and correctly sized; if a fixture is missing from the render, swap to a model that is known to render correctly.
Kitchen appliances must use library models that are visible and correctly sized; if an appliance is missing from the render, swap to a model that is known to render correctly.
Dining tables must use library models that are visible and correctly sized; if a table is missing from the render, swap to a model that is known to render correctly.
Appliances must use library models that are visible and correctly sized; if an appliance is missing from the render, swap to a model that is known to render correctly.
Desks in children's rooms should use models that are appropriate for the room's function; if a desk is missing from the render, swap to a model that is known to render correctly.
Shoe cabinets must use library models that are visible and correctly sized; if a shoe cabinet is missing from the render, swap to a model that is known to render correctly.
A piece placed by the fit stage must not stand in the approach of a window or door on the same wall; the fit stage must clear the opening's sightline before it reports the room as fitted.
A 2.15 m opening in an outer wall with no swing arc and no outside landing (furniture across its approach) is a window, not a door; the reading stage must classify it as a window at the floor's sill.
A gap in an outer wall of a wet room with furniture across its approach and no outside landing is a window, not a door; the reading stage must classify it as a window at the floor's sill.
A gap in an outer wall with the kitchen counter across its approach and no outside landing is a window, not a door; the reading stage must classify it as a window at the floor's sill.
A gap in an outer wall with furniture across its full width and no outside landing is a window, not a door; the reading stage must classify it as a window at the floor's sill.
A gap in an outer wall with furniture across its approach and no outside landing is a window, not a door; the reading stage must classify it as a window at the floor's sill.
A 2.15 m opening in an outer wall with no swing arc and furniture across its approach is a window, not a door; the reading stage must classify it as a window at the floor's sill.
A 0.65 m opening in an outer wall with furniture across its full width and no outside landing is a window, not a door; the reading stage must classify it as a window at the floor's sill.
A 1.55 m opening in an outer wall with no swing arc and furniture across its approach is a window, not a door; the reading stage must classify it as a window at the floor's sill.
The fit stage must not leave two drawn pieces overlapping; when a drawn fixture (bathtub) is kept, the other drawn piece must be moved to a free place in the room.
The big loop must run at least one full cycle before it stops; a stop with 0 cycles and no deadline means the loop did not do its job.
An interior camera marked for review must be re-posed to show the room's main furniture set, not a bare wall or a single fixture.

When a tall storage piece (wardrobe, tall cabinet) in a small room blocks an opening and no free wall span exists within the move tolerance, the solver must swap to a narrower model that fits the clear span, not attempt to move the piece to a non-existent free place.

When a low storage piece (dresser, sideboard) in a bedroom stands in front of a window and blocks the sill, and no free wall span exists within the move tolerance, the solver must swap to a model that clears the window sill height, or the architect must raise the window sill.
When a kitchen room's kitchen_run group is missing key fixtures (fridge, stove, sink), the solver must complete the group with the missing pieces, not attempt to relayout the room.

When a bed in a bedroom with a sloped ceiling has its headboard not against a wall and no free wall span exists within the move tolerance, the solver must swap to a lower-profile bed model that fits under the sloped ceiling, or the architect must adjust the ceiling height.

When a washing machine in a bathroom is rendered as a flat panel (not a recognizable appliance), the solver must swap to a proper washing machine model with a visible door and controls, not a generated model with guessed units.
When a storage room (soyunma odası) is bare and empty, the solver must place a dressing group in it, including a mirror, a hanging rail, and a garment on a hook, to match the reference.
An exterior view of a large window that opens onto a flat, empty green field must have a believable outdoor scene with depth, planters, or detail, not a void.
A terrace and the base of a facade that are bare concrete and wood with no planters or greenery must have planters or greenery to soften the transition to the lawn.
A camera view of a children's room that shows a generic, empty master bedroom must be re-posed to show the room's main pieces (wardrobe, desk, office chair) and styling layers (rug, wall art).
When a children's room has a bare wood floor, the solver must place a rug to define the sleeping or play zone, matching the reference.
When a dresser in a children's room has a completely empty top, the solver must place decorative objects (lamps, frames, plants) on it to match the reference.
When a children's room has a bare wood floor, the solver must place a soft, colorful rug to define the play/sleep zone and match the reference's warmth.
A bathroom camera view that shows a bare, unstyled shell must be re-posed to show the room's main fixtures (bathtub, toilet, washbasin) and styling layers (towel warmer, mirror).
When a bathroom lacks warm light, the solver must add a warm light source (e.g., a warm-toned ceiling light or a wall sconce) to match the reference.
A bathroom camera view that shows a bare, unstyled shell with a missing washbasin must be re-posed to show the room's main fixtures (bathtub, toilet, washbasin) and styling layers.
A room typed as a child's room must be furnished with a child-appropriate set (scaled bed, playful palette, age-appropriate decor); a generic adult bedroom set is a mismatch of the room's program.
An interior camera must frame the room's main functional group, not a corner or a single fixture; a close-up of a partition is not a room presentation.
A bad camera is fixed by re-aiming the camera, not by moving the furniture to fit the camera.
A bathroom must be styled with warm materials, texture, and lived-in details (mirrors, wood, plants, lighting); a flat untextured 'grey box' is not client-ready.
A shower enclosure model must be a clean, stylish glass partition, not a visual mess of vertical bars and reflections that looks like a construction error.
Chairs in a room must form a cohesive set matching the room's aesthetic; three different styles clashing with the bed and reference is a mismatched set.
A floor lamp must match the room's warm, paper-lantern style; a generic modern tripod does not provide the soft, warm ambient lighting the reference establishes.
Windows in a bedroom must be softened with fabric (curtains) to match the reference's warm, layered aesthetic; bare glass is a missing layer.
A hall must be styled with functional furniture (shoe cabinet, bench, hooks), wall art, lighting, and warm materials; a bare, unfinished landing is not client-ready.
A hall must contain the functional furniture shown in the reference (shoe cabinet, bench, hooks); an empty hall is a missing layer.
An interior camera must frame the room's main group, not a corner and a door; a close-up of a wall corner is not a room presentation.
A bad camera is fixed by re-aiming the camera, not by changing the room type.
Walls in a bedroom must have decorative elements (wall art) to match the reference's warm, layered aesthetic; completely bare walls are a missing layer.
A bedroom must be styled with soft furnishings, decor, and texture to match the reference's warm, organic, and layered standard; a stark, unfinished 'grey box' is not client-ready.
An interior camera must frame the room's space and its contents, not be pressed against a piece of furniture; a view that is 80% white paneling and a door leaf is not a room presentation.

An interior camera of a small room (under 8 m2) must frame the room's main furniture and at least one wall, never a bare wall or a door; if no free point shows the furniture, the view is removed, not kept.
A covered outdoor space (veranda, terrace, balcony) larger than 4 m2 must carry at least one seating group (table and chairs) so it reads as usable, not an empty shell.
Exterior renders must carry a sun (azimuth and elevation), a ground material and at least a few trees or a hedge; a flat overcast void with lollipop trees is a grey-box, not a presentation.
Exterior and window views must carry a sun so that windows show interior light or reflection; dark, flat windows read as an unfinished shell.
A decor item that cannot rest on its host (penetration or gap beyond tolerance) is dropped, not forced; the host furniture is still built and the room is not incomplete.

A drawn piece whose footprint is 60% or more inside another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece (a sink bowl, an appliance front, a lamp base) and is not a piece of its own; the AI naming of such a detail must not override the containment rule.
The reading stage must read ATTDEF entities (attribute definitions) in DWG files; they often carry room labels, dimensions or furniture tags that the ledger checks.

Site decor read on a level other than the ground floor (L0) is not used for the site (the site is the ground floor's); the reading must tag site items with their level and the site stage must only use L0 items.

When a room outline holds two labels (e.g. 'Salon' and 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ'), the reading must check whether a wall separates the two labelled areas; if not, the second label is a sub-zone of the first room, not a room of its own, and the room's area is the sum of both.

Every printed area label in the documents must be matched to a room in the model; if the label's area does not match any room's area, the reading must flag it for review rather than silently dropping it.
When the wall-layer evidence already closes the labelled rooms, off-layer wall primitives on the runner-up layer are duplicates, not lost walls; do not flag them as a loss.
Decor symbols read outside the upper floor's walls that repeat the ground plan's symbols at the same place are the ground floor's site, not lost items of the upper floor.
Furniture layers (bathtub, sink, etc.) whose item is already built in the model are not lost building elements; do not flag their raw line entities as unused.

When one room outline holds two labels and the second is a sub-zone (dining, antre) with no separating wall, the reading must keep the larger label and record the sub-zone as a zone of the room, not as a lost room; the building stage must not expect a separate room for it.

When a drawn piece is a few centimetres off its drawn place and the current model's footprint prevents a tighter fit, swap to a model whose footprint matches the drawn size so the fit solver can re-seat it.

When a drawn dresser (or similar low storage) is placed in front of a window and no other free wall span exists within 1.2 m of its drawn centre, the layout stage must accept the drawn position and the check must raise the tolerance for pieces drawn in front of windows, or the architect must move the window.

When a drawn wardrobe is placed in front of a window and no other free wall span exists, the layout stage must accept the drawn position and the check must raise the tolerance for pieces drawn in front of windows, or the architect must move the window.

When an elevation has no north arrow or view bearing, the reading stage must record the elevation's side from the plan's axis grid or section marks, or the check must skip the elevation-to-plan comparison and flag it as 'not checkable' rather than 'could not run'.

When a drawn section's ends do not align with the plan's roof outline (over 0.30 m apart), the check must skip the point-by-point comparison and flag the section as 'not aligned with plan' rather than 'could not run'.

guards.rule: When a shoe_cabinet (or similar entrance furniture) in a hall blocks a door and no free position exists that clears the door swing and other fixed elements, the agent must remove the piece (it is not essential) rather than retrying moves, and the layout stage must not place entrance furniture in a door swing.
When no library model of the building's window family fits the opening's size, the parametric opening in the style's finish is the correct fallback; do not flag it as a missing model.
When no library model of a window family fits the drawn size, the parametric opening in the style's finish is the correct build, not a defect.
When a fitting is built below the library level, swap to a library model that fits the piece's size and the room's style.
When no library model of a wall_cabinet fits the drawn size, the parametric mesh is the correct build; the library should be expanded to include more wall_cabinet sizes.
When a washbasin looks unstyled and clashes with the room's aesthetic, swap to a library model that matches the style and fits the size.
When kitchen cabinetry looks like a plain, flat white placeholder, set the material to a warm wood tone that matches the reference.
When a fridge looks like a generic, industrial placeholder, swap to a library model that matches the room's warm, wood-and-white aesthetic.
When a coffee table looks like a generic, low-poly placeholder, swap to a library model with more detail and material richness.
Curtains and other soft window treatments are not part of the furniture library; the pipeline should either add them to the library or the finding should be marked as out of scope.
When a bedroom lacks bedside lighting, add the missing functional group (e.g. sleeping_single) that includes a nightstand and lamp.
When a washbasin looks unstyled with exposed plumbing, swap to a library model with an integrated look.
Cushions, throws, and other soft bedding layers are not part of the furniture library; the pipeline should either add them to the library or the finding should be marked as out of scope.
Styled surfaces (books, small decor) are not part of the furniture library; the pipeline should either add them to the library or the finding should be marked as out of scope.
When a stair railing looks like a generic, industrial placeholder, set the material to a warm wood tone that matches the project's style.
Bed models in the library must include bedding (mattress, pillows, duvet) and a throw as part of the asset; a bare frame is not an acceptable bed model for any style.
Windows in living and bedroom rooms must be furnished with curtains or blinds as part of the room's decor set; bare windows are not acceptable for a furnished render.
Interior doors must use a styled model (panelled, flush with hardware detail) matching the project's style; a plain flat slab is not acceptable for a furnished render.
When a piece is removed by an explicit AI.remove_piece action, the build stage must not flag its absence as a conservation loss; the removal is a valid design decision.

Drawn clusters exceeding 4.5 m in length that do not match standard furniture dimensions should be treated as architectural built-ins or wall units, not as individual furniture pieces, and excluded from the parametric furniture build.
Drawn marks thinner than 0.2 m that do not fit any furniture type should be treated as architectural details (e.g., taps, valves, thresholds) and not built as furniture.
Drawn marks that are 60% or more contained within another piece of furniture should be treated as details of that piece (e.g., pillows, blankets) and not built as separate furniture.
When a nightstand cannot be placed without cutting the bed, the build stage should attempt to swap to a smaller or differently shaped nightstand model before marking it as not built.
When a shoe_cabinet cannot be placed without blocking a door, the build stage should attempt to swap to a smaller or differently shaped shoe_cabinet model before marking it as not built.
The upper end of a stair that leads to the top floor should not be built again as a separate piece; it is already represented by the stair on the lower floor.
Decorative elements that depend on a host piece should not be flagged as lost if the host piece is being addressed by a fix; they will be built once the host is built.
Decorative elements that depend on a host piece that was intentionally removed should not be flagged as lost; they are correctly not built.

When a site area (veranda, balcony, terrace) is identified in the drawing with a label and outline, the build stage must construct its floor slab, edge, and any drawn steps or guard rails as part of the site model, even if the area is not a room.

When a room contains a labeled sub-zone (e.g., 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ' for dining) that is large enough to be a functional area, the reading stage should either split the room into two rooms (living + dining) or type the room as 'living' with a dining group placed within it, ensuring the dining table and chairs are in the same room as the dining zone label.
A piece whose type was inferred from context and is already built and consistent with its neighbours is not a defect; the inference log is informational.

When a drawn furniture label is present but the solver cannot place the piece within 1 m of the label due to room congestion, the system should either (a) relax the placement tolerance to 2 m for storage pieces in bedrooms, or (b) automatically trigger a relayout of the room to free up space near the label before attempting placement.

An outer opening that is blocked by furniture such that it cannot function as a passage should be reclassified as a window if its dimensions and position are consistent with a window (e.g., sill height, width) and there is no other door providing access to that part of the facade.
A room with an area less than 3 m2 and type 'hall' or 'stair' is not expected to contain furniture; the absence of furniture is not a defect.
Furniture that blocks a window or door opening must be moved to a free position in the room that does not obstruct the opening.
A labelled outdoor extension (veranda, terrace, balcony) in the documents must be built as a platform with its own floor, roof, and glazing, not ignored.
A room under 3 m2 with no fixtures is a hall or storage, not a room.
A kitchen must have a functional run with a sink, hob, and fridge, not just bare counters.
A living room with a dining area must have a dining table and chairs.
A children's room should have age-appropriate furniture, such as a bunk bed or single beds, not adult double beds.
Site areas labelled in the plan (veranda, balcony, terrace) must be built as floor slabs with railings or glazing, not skipped when they lack a closed wall outline.
A room typed as a children's bedroom must be furnished with child-appropriate furniture (bunk beds, cribs, single beds), not standard double beds.
A kitchen room must have a complete functional run including a sink, hob/stove, and counter space, not just bare counter boxes.
A living room (salon) that is programmed to include a dining area must have a dining table and chairs placed in it.
A bathroom room must have its main fixtures (bathtub, toilet, washbasin) placed and visible, not just listed in the room's pieces.
A hall or entrance room must have its main functional piece (e.g., shoe cabinet, console table) placed and visible.
null

Furniture strokes on the 'tefriş' layer that form recognizable sets (e.g., sofa with chairs) must be read as individual pieces even if they are not explicitly labeled, to prevent loss of drawn furniture.

The main functional piece of a room (e.g., bed in a bedroom) must always be built and visible; if it is listed in the room's pieces but not visible in the render, the build stage must be rerun or the piece re-placed.
Site areas labeled in the documents (e.g., VERANDA, BALKON) must be built with outlines and structures if they are part of the building's program, not just open slabs.

A storage room whose program is a dressing set must have its wardrobe placed by the fitting stage; when the solver reports no place, the stage must retry with the room's free spans before the piece is left unbuilt.
A bathroom or WC room that lists a washing machine must have it placed by the fitting stage; the group solver must not reject the room type when the piece is explicitly in the room's program.

A bathroom's main fixtures (bathtub, toilet, washbasin) must all be placed and visible; the fitting stage must verify that each listed piece is built and at its correct working height before the room is marked complete.

A hall's main piece (shoe cabinet) must be placed by the fitting stage; when a relayout is refused due to walkway constraints, the fit stage must find an alternative position that satisfies both the piece placement and the circulation requirement.
A hall's main piece (shoe cabinet) must be placed by the fitting stage; the room type is already correct, so the issue is purely a placement failure.
A bedroom's main piece (bed) must be placed by the fitting stage; the room is 11.3 m2 and the bed_single is listed, so the fit stage must place it.
A small hall or entry room's main piece (shoe cabinet) must be placed by the fitting stage; the room type attempts were no-ops, so the issue is purely a placement failure.
A bathroom render must show all three main fixtures (bathtub, toilet, washbasin); the camera must be positioned to include all of them in frame.

A dining table in a kitchen must use a model that matches the project's style chain (scandinavian -> minimal -> modern) and fits the room's dimensions; the current model is industrial style and not built.
A washing machine must use a real product model that fits within the room's dimensions and matches the project's style; generated models with guessed units are not acceptable.
A bathroom or WC render must show all main fixtures; the camera must be positioned to include the washbasin, toilet, and shower in frame.
A hall render must show its main piece (shoe cabinet); the camera must be positioned to include the shoe cabinet in frame.
A window opening must not be blocked by furniture; the build stage must verify that no piece obstructs the ray through any opening.
An opening in the outer wall that is blocked by furniture and has no passage function should be read as a window, not a door; the reading stage must check for furniture blocking the approach.

A warning that an opening is 'no passage, read as a window' is a false alarm when the project facts already list that opening id under the floor's windows: the reading correction is applied and the warning is stale.
When a drawn fixture clashes with another drawn piece in a wet room, the drawn fixture is kept and the other piece is moved to a free place in the room.
A piece that stands across the approach of a window and covers the opening is moved clear of the window.
When the big loop stops with no gain after a single cycle, rerun the stage to allow more cycles to raise the house score.
A view marked for review is moved to a free point that shows the room's key pieces.

When a wardrobe in a small storage room blocks a window and no free place on the wall clears it, the wardrobe is removed from the room (it does not belong there) and the room is re-typed or the window is re-read.
When a dresser's back is not on a wall and no free place on the wall is within 1.2 m of the drawn place, the dresser is moved to the nearest free place in the room, clear of the doorway or window.

A kitchen run group is not complete until its required appliances (fridge, stove/hob, sink) are present and fitted; the group check must fail the layout (and block relayout) until the missing appliance is placed, so the agent is forced to add the missing piece rather than re-arranging the bare counter.
A dining area (table with chairs) in a kitchen or living room must be grounded by a rug; the furniture agent adds one when the reference shows a patterned area rug.
Kitchen counters must use models that match the project's material palette (e.g., wood fronts, stone tops) rather than generic parametric boxes.
Appliances must use models that match the project's finish (matte, natural) rather than high-gloss generic assets.
Kitchen renders must show a fully styled space with warm lighting, decor, and a complete dining set, not a bare shell.
Kitchen renders must show all functional elements (wall cabinets, dining set) and decor to match the reference style.
Living room furniture must form a coherent set with a unified style, and the room must be styled with soft layers (rugs, cushions) to match the reference.
Sofas in a living room must match the style of the other main seating pieces to form a coherent set.
Living rooms must be styled with soft textiles (cushions, throws) on seating to match the reference's warm, layered look.
Living room renders must show a coherent, styled space with unified furniture and soft furnishings, not a bare shell.
Living room renders must show a 'lived-in' space with rugs, art, and soft furnishings to match the reference.
Dining areas must be grounded by a rug to define the space and match the reference style.
Armchairs in a living room must match the style of the other main seating pieces to form a coherent set.
Bathroom renders must show a styled space with soft furnishings and all required fixtures (including the washing machine) to match the reference.
Bathroom lighting must be warm and inviting, not flat and clinical, to match the reference style.
Child's rooms must be styled with playful, warm, and functional elements to match the reference, not as a generic master bedroom.
A room's furniture set must match its named function and age group; a children's room must not be furnished as a generic adult master bedroom.
A single children's room should not contain two double beds; the furniture set must be appropriate for the room's size and function.
Room styling must reflect the room's specific function and user demographic; a children's room requires playful and warm decor.
Interior cameras must frame the main functional pieces of the room, not just corners or secondary fixtures.
Bathroom styling should include a mix of textures (e.g., wood, stone) to avoid a sterile, flat appearance.
Bathrooms must include functional details (mirrors, towel storage) and styling to feel like a designed space.
Bedrooms should include plants (hanging or potted) to add warmth and life to the space.
Furniture models must match the room's overall style; a mid-century armchair clashes with a Scandinavian bedroom.
Halls should include functional and stylistic elements (shoe cabinet, wall art, lighting, rug) to feel like a designed space.
Halls should include a shoe cabinet and bench to address their main function as an entryway.
Interior cameras must frame the room and its main furniture, not just corners or doors.
Bedrooms should include wall art to add visual interest and avoid bare walls.
Bedrooms should include soft furnishings and decor to feel warm and lived-in.
An interior camera of a small storage or hall room must frame the room's main furniture group, not a door leaf or a bare wall corner.
The exterior site must include a path and a front court (planting/hardscape) to soften the transition from the facade to the ground.
Exterior renders must include warm interior light (windows glowing) and exterior fixtures so the house does not read as an unlit shell.
A decor item that cannot rest on its host without penetration is correctly not built; the host model's surface is the cause.
A decor item that cannot rest on its host without sufficient support is correctly not built; the host model's surface is the cause.
A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece's footprint is treated as a detail of that piece, not a piece of its own, even if an AI pass names it a separate type.
The reading stage must read ATTDEF entities in DWG files to capture block attribute definitions that may hold room labels or dimensions.
Site decor read on upper levels (L1+) that repeats ground plan symbols at the same place is not used, as the site belongs to the ground floor (L0).
A shoe_cabinet in a hall must be placed on a wall span that is not the swing or clearance zone of any door in that hall; if no such span exists, the piece is not built rather than blocking a door.
Wall cabinets in a kitchen must be built with a library model if one is available; if no library model fits, the parametric mesh is acceptable but should be flagged for review.
Windows in bedrooms and living areas should have curtains or blinds added as a decor layer to match the reference style.
Plants in the foreground of a render should be chosen to match the organic, trailing style of the reference, avoiding stiff, uniform 'lollipop' looks.
Interior doors should have some detail or contrast (e.g., panels, handles, or a different finish) to avoid looking like flat, unadorned slabs.
Nightstands and other small surfaces should have styled decor (e.g., books, small objects) to make the space feel personal and curated.
Window and door surrounds must be given a finished frame material (wood or painted) matching the project's style, never left as a plain white parametric box.
The approach path and door landing must be given a defined paving material (a landing or material change at the door), not a single bare slab.
Exterior renders must use a warm, believable sun (not a flat grey overcast void) so the home reads as a styled, lit residence.
An opening read twice (the same opening detected on two passes) is built once; the duplicate read is not a loss.
Structural grid bubbles (axis labels) and drawing annotations are not built; they are drawing marks, not house elements.
A cushion, pillow or detail drawn on a piece is part of that piece, not a piece of its own; it is not built separately.
A column drawn on 'KOLON' that is a post of a veranda is built as part of that veranda structure, not as a separate lost element.
Level mark symbols (kot) are drawing annotations, not built elements.
An exterior label whose surface is built from site paving/parking/grass is not a lost element; the surface is built as site ground.
One object read twice (two outlines of the same kitchen counter) is built once; the duplicate is not a loss.
A piece drawn inside another piece (60% or more) is the same piece drawn twice or a part of it; it is not built separately.
A kitchen run drawn as one outline with its fixtures is replaced by its counter legs along the walls; the run is built as its parts, not as one outline.
An outline around other pieces (a rug or zone outline) is not a piece; rugs are laid under the groups by the decor rules.
A dining table whose model is not in the project's style chain must be swapped to a model that is in the chain (scandinavian/minimal/modern) and fits the piece's size.
A 'not built' finding whose reason is 'the answer to AI.remove_piece' is a false alarm: the removal was an intentional edit, not a stage dropping a drawn element.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side is not a single furniture piece; it is either a wall, a built-in, or a misread. The build stage is correct to not build it as a single parametric piece.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m is a detail (tap, valve, threshold, shelf line), not a furniture piece. The build stage is correct to not build it as a piece.
A drawn mark that is 60% or more inside another piece is a detail of that piece, not a separate piece. The build stage is correct to not build it as a separate item.

When a nightstand cannot be placed without cutting the bed and no free place is found within 1.0 m, the nightstand should be removed or the bed should be moved to make space, rather than leaving the nightstand unbuilt.
A stair that arrives from a lower level and has no level above is not built again on the upper level. This is correct behavior for a stair that terminates at the top floor.
When a host piece is not built due to a spatial conflict, the decorations on it should also be removed or the host should be moved to make space, rather than leaving both unbuilt.
When a host piece is removed by an explicit action, the decorations on it should also be removed, rather than leaving them unbuilt.
A decorative element whose host piece is not built is not a conservation loss; it is dropped with its host.
A door symbol on a symbol layer is a drawing annotation, not a built element; it is not a conservation loss.
A hatch on a hatching layer is a drawing annotation, not a built element; it is not a conservation loss.
An outdoor-space edge or step detail is built with its host outdoor space; it is not a separate conservation loss.

When the building frame is offset from the sheet outline corner, the reading must anchor the model to the sheet frame (or record the offset) so that all regions and coordinates are consistent with the sheet, not with an arbitrary corner.
When the section prints the ground floor at a non-zero level (e.g. +0.50), the reading must shift the plan level marks by that offset so that building z 0 matches the printed datum.
A small drawn piece around a level-mark text is a level-mark symbol, not furniture; it must be marked as such, not built.
A furniture name text that matches an already-built piece in the room is not a loss; it is accounted for.
A furniture name text in a room that does not have that piece is a reading note; it is not a conservation loss unless the documents show the piece should be there.
A zone label within a room (e.g. 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ' in a living room) is a sub-zone, not a separate room; the reading must not treat it as a second room label.
A piece typed by context (size, position, orientation relative to a table) is a correct reading, not a loss.

A drawn furniture label whose nearest valid placement in its room is more than 1 m from the text is a misread or a label for a piece outside the room: do not add a piece at the text position, and flag the label for manual review instead of silently dropping it.

A labelled outdoor area (veranda, terrace, balcony) that the plan outlines and the model partially builds must be registered as a site area with its own floor, railing and furniture set, not left as unbounded ad-hoc geometry.
A sub-3 m2 enclosed space with no fixtures and no door of its own is not a room; it must be re-typed as a hall/landing or merged into the adjacent room, never left as a doorless 'other' room.

A kitchen room must be built as a complete, working run (counter + sink + hob + worktop) as one group; a kitchen whose counters are bare boxes with no sink or hob is a failed kitchen run, not a furnished kitchen.

A living room whose program includes a dining set must have that set placed as a coherent group (table + chairs) in the room; a dining table listed in the program but absent from the room is a lost dining group.
A bathroom room must be built as a complete set (bathtub or shower + toilet + washbasin) as one group; a bathroom whose main fixture (bathtub/shower) is listed but absent is a failed bathroom set.

A children's room programmed for one child must have exactly one bed; a second double bed in a single-child room is a misread or duplicate sleeping piece and must be re-typed to a single bed or removed.
A floor should have one main hall; a second sub-4 m2 'hall' with a shoe cabinet is a misread entrance or landing and must be re-typed (storage, hall-landing) or merged into the main hall.

A labelled outdoor area (veranda, balcony, terrace) that the plan outlines must be built as a platform with its own floor and glazing/railing; 'no outline' is a read failure, not a valid reason to drop it.
A small interior room (under ~5 m2) that holds a shoe cabinet or wardrobe and has no entrance door is a storage/utility room, not a hall; retype it so its furniture and access make sense.
A room labelled dressing/soyunma must carry a dressing set (mirror, bench, chest) in addition to its wardrobe; a lone wardrobe is not a dressing room.
A shoe cabinet belongs at the entrance hall of the ground floor, not in an upper-floor hall; an upper hall's storage anchor is a console or coat stand.

Site areas labeled as 'VERANDA' or 'BALKON' in the plan must be explicitly built as distinct site elements with their own geometry (deck, posts, roof) and linked to the corresponding interior doors, rather than being absorbed into the main building volume or ignored.
Site areas defined in the plan (like balconies or verandas) must be built if they are indicated by railings or doors, even if the 'outline' flag is missing.

evidence.rule: A sub-3 m2 enclosed space with no fixtures and no door of its own is not a room; it must be re-typed as a hall/landing or merged into the adjacent room, never left as a doorless 'other' room.

findings.message: The kitchen (24.8 m2) is functionally empty in the render: the counters are bare white boxes with no sink, no hob and no visible worktop, even though the room's piece list includes sink_kitchen, stove and kitchen_counter. The kitchen run was not assembled as a working set, so the room reads as a storage box rather than a kitchen.

evidence.rule: A kitchen room must be built as a complete, working run (counter + sink + hob + worktop) as one group; a kitchen whose counters are bare boxes with no sink or hob is a failed kitchen run, not a furnished kitchen.

findings.message: The salon is missing its dining set: the room's program lists table_dining and chairs, but the dining table and chairs are not visible in the render and are not placed as a coherent set. The salon therefore reads as a living room only, with the dining function lost.

evidence.rule: A living room whose program includes a dining set must have that set placed as a coherent group (table + chairs) in the room; a dining table listed in the program but absent from the room is a lost dining group.

findings.message: The L0 bathroom is missing its main piece, the bathtub (f_L0_010), which is listed in the room's pieces but not visible in the render. A bathroom without its bathtub reads as a WC, not a bathroom.

evidence.rule: A bathroom room must be built as a complete set (bathtub or shower + toilet + washbasin) as one group; a bathroom whose main fixture (bathtub/shower) is listed but absent is a failed bathroom set.

findings.message: The L1 bathroom is missing its main piece, the bathtub (f_L1_009), which is listed in the room's pieces but not visible in the render. A bathroom without its bathtub reads as a WC, not a bathroom.

evidence.rule: A bathroom room must be built as a complete set (bathtub or shower + toilet + washbasin) as one group; a bathroom whose main fixture (bathtub/shower) is listed but absent is a failed bathroom set.

findings.message: A second double bed (f_L1_007) is placed in the corner of the children's room, which is illogical for a single child's room and was cut by the architect (F5) but the loss is not resolved: the room still has two double beds in its piece list (bed_double appears twice) and the cut left the room's sleeping set inconsistent.

evidence.rule: A children's room programmed for one child must have exactly one bed; a second double bed in a single-child room is a misread or duplicate sleeping piece and must be re-typed to a single bed or removed.

findings.message: r_L1_oda is typed 'hall' (3.1 m2) and holds a shoe_cabinet, but it is a small interior room on L1 with no entrance door and no clear function; a shoe cabinet in a 3 m2 interior hall makes no sense and the room is unreachable as a hall.

evidence.rule: A floor should have one main hall; a second sub-4 m2 'hall' with a shoe cabinet is a misread entrance or landing and must be re-typed (storage, hall-landing) or merged into the main hall.

also: r_L1_oda is a 3.1 m2 hall with a shoe_cabinet, but it is the only 'hall' on L1 besides r_L1_hol (11.0 m2, also a hall with a shoe_cabinet and the stair). Two halls on the same floor, one of them 3.1 m2 with a shoe cabinet, is a misread: the 3.1 m2 space is most likely a small entrance/antre or a stair landing, not a second hall.

findings.message: r_L1_soyunma_odasi (storage, 5.9 m2) holds only a wardrobe and is labelled 'Soyunma Odası' (dressing room); a dressing room with a single wardrobe and no mirror or bench is functionally empty and reads as a dead storage box.

evidence.rule: A room labelled dressing/soyunma must carry a dressing set (mirror, bench, chest) in addition to its wardrobe; a lone wardrobe is not a dressing room.

findings.message: r_L1_hol (hall, 11.0 m2) holds a shoe_cabinet and a stair, but a shoe cabinet in an upper-floor hall is illogical (shoes are stored at the entrance on L0); the hall's main anchor should be the stair and a console, not a shoe cabinet.

evidence.rule: A shoe cabinet belongs at the entrance hall of the ground floor, not in an upper-floor hall; an upper hall's storage anchor is a console or coat stand.

findings.message: visitor (outdoor:os_L0_veranda): The veranda (os_L0_veranda) is not built. The facts state 'site area sa_L0_veranda 'VERANDA' (other): NOT built (no outline)'. In the 3D model (Image 1), there is a covered outdoor area with a deck, posts, and furniture, but it is not recognized as a distinct site area in the model data. It appears to be an extension of the salon or a separate structure not linked to the 'VERANDA' label. Without the 'VERANDA' area being built, its specific attributes (guards, roof coverage as per plan) cannot be verified against the model. The visual shows a deck, but the data says it's missing.

evidence.question: The veranda 'VERANDA' (os_L0_veranda): from which door does a person step onto it; does every open edge over a drop have a guard; is it covered where a veranda should be (and where the roof plan covers it); does it read as a veranda (its floor, ceiling, posts, furniture, lights) or as something else (a carport, a bare slab, a roof)?
evidence.rule: Site areas labeled as 'VERANDA' or 'BALKON' in the plan must be explicitly built as distinct site elements with their own geometry (deck, posts, roof) and linked to the corresponding interior doors, rather than being absorbed into the main building volume or ignored.

findings.message: visitor (outdoor:os_L1_balkon): The balcony 'BALKON' (os_L1_balkon) is not built. The site area is listed as 'NOT built (no outline)'. While there is a glass railing visible on the upper floor in the 3D model, the actual balcony floor and structure are missing from the built model, leaving an open edge or a void where the balcony should be.

evidence.question: The balcony 'BALKON' (os_L1_balkon): from which door does a person step onto it; does every open edge over a drop have a guard; is it covered where a balcony should be (and where the roof plan covers it); does it read as a balcony (its floor, ceiling, posts, furniture, lights) or as something else (a carport, a bare slab, a roof)?
evidence.rule: Site areas defined in the plan (like balconies or verandas) must be built if they are indicated by railings or doors, even if the 'outline' flag is missing.
evidence.value: Site areas marked as 'NOT built' in the project facts must be constructed if they are part of the architectural design (e.g., a balcony with a railing).

rules_proposed.rule: When a storage room (soyunma odası) is bare and empty, the solver must place a dressing group in it, including a mirror, a hanging rail, and a garment on a hook, to match the reference.
An exterior view of a large window that opens onto a flat, empty green field must have a believable outdoor scene with depth, planters, or detail, not a void.
A terrace and the base of a facade that are bare concrete and wood with no planters or greenery must have planters or greenery to soften the transition to the lawn.
A camera view of a children's room that shows a generic, empty master bedroom must be re-posed to show the room's main pieces (wardrobe, desk, office chair) and styling layers (rug, wall art).
When a children's room has a bare wood floor, the solver must place a rug to define the sleeping or play zone, matching the reference.
When a dresser in a children's room has a completely empty top, the solver must place decorative objects (lamps, frames, plants) on it to match the reference.
When a children's room has a bare wood floor, the solver must place a soft, colorful rug to define the play/sleep zone and match the reference's warmth.
A bathroom camera view that shows a bare, unstyled shell must be re-posed to show the room's main fixtures (bathtub, toilet, washbasin) and styling layers (towel warmer, mirror).
When a bathroom lacks warm light, the solver must add a warm light source (e.g., a warm-toned ceiling light or a wall sconce) to match the reference.
A bathroom camera view that shows a bare, unstyled shell with a missing washbasin must be re-posed to show the room's main fixtures (bathtub, toilet, washbasin) and styling layers.
A room typed as a child's room must be furnished with a child-appropriate set (scaled bed, playful palette, age-appropriate decor); a generic adult bedroom set is a mismatch of the room's program.
An interior camera must frame the room's main functional group, not a corner or a single fixture; a close-up of a partition is not a room presentation.
A bad camera is fixed by re-aiming the camera, not by moving the furniture to fit the camera.
A bathroom must be styled with warm materials, texture, and lived-in details (mirrors, wood, plants, lighting); a flat untextured 'grey box' is not client-ready.
A shower enclosure model must be a clean, stylish glass partition, not a visual mess of vertical bars and reflections that looks like a construction error.
Chairs in a room must form a cohesive set matching the room's aesthetic; three different styles clashing with the bed and reference is a mismatched set.
A floor lamp must match the room's warm, paper-lantern style; a generic modern tripod does not provide the soft, warm ambient lighting the reference establishes.
Windows in a bedroom must be softened with fabric (curtains) to match the reference's warm, layered aesthetic; bare glass is a missing layer.
A hall must be styled with functional furniture (shoe cabinet, bench, hooks), wall art, lighting, and warm materials; a bare, unfinished landing is not client-ready.
A hall must contain the functional furniture shown in the reference (shoe cabinet, bench, hooks); an empty hall is a missing layer.
An interior camera must frame the room's main group, not a corner and a door; a close-up of a wall corner is not a room presentation.
A bad camera is fixed by re-aiming the camera, not by changing the room type.
Walls in a bedroom must have decorative elements (wall art) to match the reference's warm, layered aesthetic; completely bare walls are a missing layer.
A bedroom must be styled with soft furnishings, decor, and texture to match the reference's warm, organic, and layered standard; a stark, unfinished 'grey box' is not client-ready.
An interior camera must frame the room's space and its contents, not be pressed against a piece of furniture; a view that is 80% white paneling and a door leaf is not a room presentation.

An interior camera of a small room (under 8 m2) must frame the room's main furniture and at least one wall, never a bare wall or a door; if no free point shows the furniture, the view is removed, not kept.
A covered outdoor space (veranda, terrace, balcony) larger than 4 m2 must carry at least one seating group (table and chairs) so it reads as usable, not an empty shell.
Exterior renders must carry a sun (azimuth and elevation), a ground material and at least a few trees or a hedge; a flat overcast void with lollipop trees is a grey-box, not a presentation.
Exterior and window views must carry a sun so that windows show interior light or reflection; dark, flat windows read as an unfinished shell.
When no library model of the building's window family fits the opening's size, the parametric opening in the style's finish is the correct fallback; do not flag it as a missing model.
When no library model of a window family fits the drawn size, the parametric opening in the style's finish is the correct build, not a defect.
When a fitting is built below the library level, swap to a library model that fits the piece's size and the room's style.
When no library model of a wall_cabinet fits the drawn size, the parametric mesh is the correct build; the library should be expanded to include more wall_cabinet sizes.
When a washbasin looks unstyled and clashes with the room's aesthetic, swap to a library model that matches the style and fits the size.
When kitchen cabinetry looks like a plain, flat white placeholder, set the material to a warm wood tone that matches the reference.
When a fridge looks like a generic, industrial placeholder, swap to a library model that matches the room's warm, wood-and-white aesthetic.
When a coffee table looks like a generic, low-poly placeholder, swap to a library model with more detail and material richness.
Curtains and other soft window treatments are not part of the furniture library; the pipeline should either add them to the library or the finding should be marked as out of scope.
When a bedroom lacks bedside lighting, add the missing functional group (e.g. sleeping_single) that includes a nightstand and lamp.
When a washbasin looks unstyled with exposed plumbing, swap to a library model with an integrated look.
Cushions, throws, and other soft bedding layers are not part of the furniture library; the pipeline should either add them to the library or the finding should be marked as out of scope.
Styled surfaces (books, small decor) are not part of the furniture library; the pipeline should either add them to the library or the finding should be marked as out of scope.
When a stair railing looks like a generic, industrial placeholder, set the material to a warm wood tone that matches the project's style.
Bed models in the library must include bedding (mattress, pillows, duvet) and a throw as part of the asset; a bare frame is not an acceptable bed model for any style.
Windows in living and bedroom rooms must be furnished with curtains or blinds as part of the room's decor set; bare windows are not acceptable for a furnished render.
Interior doors must use a styled model (panelled, flush with hardware detail) matching the project's style; a plain flat slab is not acceptable for a furnished render.
A dining area (table with chairs) in a kitchen or living room must be grounded by a rug; the furniture agent adds one when the reference shows a patterned area rug.
Kitchen counters must use models that match the project's material palette (e.g., wood fronts, stone tops) rather than generic parametric boxes.
Appliances must use models that match the project's finish (matte, natural) rather than high-gloss generic assets.
Kitchen renders must show a fully styled space with warm lighting, decor, and a complete dining set, not a bare shell.
Kitchen renders must show all functional elements (wall cabinets, dining set) and decor to match the reference style.
Living room furniture must form a coherent set with a unified style, and the room must be styled with soft layers (rugs, cushions) to match the reference.
Sofas in a living room must match the style of the other main seating pieces to form a coherent set.
Living rooms must be styled with soft textiles (cushions, throws) on seating to match the reference's warm, layered look.
Living room renders must show a coherent, styled space with unified furniture and soft furnishings, not a bare shell.
Living room renders must show a 'lived-in' space with rugs, art, and soft furnishings to match the reference.
Dining areas must be grounded by a rug to define the space and match the reference style.
Armchairs in a living room must match the style of the other main seating pieces to form a coherent set.
Bathroom renders must show a styled space with soft furnishings and all required fixtures (including the washing machine) to match the reference.
Bathroom lighting must be warm and inviting, not flat and clinical, to match the reference style.
Child's rooms must be styled with playful, warm, and functional elements to match the reference, not as a generic master bedroom.
A room's furniture set must match its named function and age group; a children's room must not be furnished as a generic adult master bedroom.
A single children's room should not contain two double beds; the furniture set must be appropriate for the room's size and function.
Room styling must reflect the room's specific function and user demographic; a children's room requires playful and warm decor.
Interior cameras must frame the main functional pieces of the room, not just corners or secondary fixtures.
Bathroom styling should include a mix of textures (e.g., wood, stone) to avoid a sterile, flat appearance.
Bathrooms must include functional details (mirrors, towel storage) and styling to feel like a designed space.
Bedrooms should include plants (hanging or potted) to add warmth and life to the space.
Furniture models must match the room's overall style; a mid-century armchair clashes with a Scandinavian bedroom.
Halls should include functional and stylistic elements (shoe cabinet, wall art, lighting, rug) to feel like a designed space.
Halls should include a shoe cabinet and bench to address their main function as an entryway.
Interior cameras must frame the room and its main furniture, not just corners or doors.
Bedrooms should include wall art to add visual interest and avoid bare walls.
Bedrooms should include soft furnishings and decor to feel warm and lived-in.
An interior camera of a small storage or hall room must frame the room's main furniture group, not a door leaf or a bare wall corner.
The exterior site must include a path and a front court (planting/hardscape) to soften the transition from the facade to the ground.
Exterior renders must include warm interior light (windows glowing) and exterior fixtures so the house does not read as an unlit shell.
Wall cabinets in a kitchen must be built with a library model if one is available; if no library model fits, the parametric mesh is acceptable but should be flagged for review.
Windows in bedrooms and living areas should have curtains or blinds added as a decor layer to match the reference style.
Plants in the foreground of a render should be chosen to match the organic, trailing style of the reference, avoiding stiff, uniform 'lollipop' looks.
Interior doors should have some detail or contrast (e.g., panels, handles, or a different finish) to avoid looking like flat, unadorned slabs.
Nightstands and other small surfaces should have styled decor (e.g., books, small objects) to make the space feel personal and curated.
Window and door surrounds must be given a finished frame material (wood or painted) matching the project's style, never left as a plain white parametric box.
The approach path and door landing must be given a defined paving material (a landing or material change at the door), not a single bare slab.
Exterior renders must use a warm, believable sun (not a flat grey overcast void) so the home reads as a styled, lit residence.
